questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: identify the medium properties that determine wave speed
questions.stem: A mechanical wave travels along a stretched string. Which choice describes what actually sets the speed of that wave?

options.text: The elastic properties and tension of the medium
The frequency that the source driver produces
options.misconception: believes a higher driver frequency makes the wave travel faster

options.text: The amplitude that the driver shakes the string
options.misconception: believes a larger amplitude increases wave speed

options.text: The loudness of the sound reaching the listener
options.misconception: confuses perceived loudness with the physical wave speed

questions.explanation: Wave speed is a property of the medium: v = sqrt(T/mu), set by tension T and linear mass density mu, so changing T or mu changes v. Frequency and amplitude are set by the source and do not enter the speed. The trap feels right because raising the driver frequency does raise the pitch, but pitch and speed are different quantities, and only the medium sets v.
questions.hint: Ask which quantities the driver controls and which the string controls.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Wave speed from distance and time
questions.learningObjective: compute wave speed from distance travelled in a time
questions.stem: A wave crest travels 12.0 m along a rope in 3.0 s at constant speed. What is the speed of the wave in metres per second? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: v = d/t = 12.0 m / 3.0 s = 4.0 m/s. Check by working backwards: 4.0 m/s multiplied by 3.0 s gives 12.0 m again. The trap is dividing the time by the distance, which gives 0.25 m per second and inverts the meaning of speed entirely.
questions.hint: Distance divided by time gives the rate of travel.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state how medium particles move in a transverse wave
questions.stem: In a transverse wave on a rope, how do the particles of the rope move relative to the direction the wave travels?

options.text: Perpendicular to the direction of travel
Parallel to the direction of travel
options.misconception: confuses transverse waves with longitudinal compression waves

options.text: Faster than the wave itself moves
options.misconception: believes particles travel along with the pulse at wave speed

options.text: In a circle around the direction of travel
options.misconception: confuses linear transverse motion with circular particle motion

questions.explanation: Transverse means the particle displacement is at right angles to the direction the wave travels, as on a rope shaken up and down. The pulse moves along the rope at speed v = d/t while each particle only oscillates about its own rest position. The trap is assuming matter travels with the wave: over 3.0 s at 4.0 m/s a point 12.0 m away is disturbed, but no particle has moved 12.0 m down the rope.
questions.hint: Name what the word transverse describes about the particle motion.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: connect perceived pitch to the frequency of a sound
questions.stem: A listener compares two steady tones sounded by different instruments at the same loudness. Which property of the sound sets the perceived pitch?

options.text: The frequency of the vibration
The amplitude of the vibration
options.misconception: believes a louder tone also sounds higher in pitch

options.text: The wavelength in the air
options.misconception: believes wavelength alone sets pitch, ignoring the frequency

options.text: The speed of sound in the air
options.misconception: confuses the propagation speed with the vibration frequency

questions.explanation: Pitch tracks frequency, so a 440 Hz tone sits below a 880 Hz tone no matter how loud either one is. In v = f times wavelength, a 340 m/s sound at 440 Hz has a wavelength of 0.77 m, so frequency and wavelength trade off while speed stays put. The trap is amplitude: doubling amplitude roughly doubles perceived loudness but leaves f, and so pitch, unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask what the ear counts per second.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: obtain wave frequency by counting cycles per second
questions.stem: A sensor on a buoy counts 15 wave crests pass it in 3.0 s. What is the frequency of the water wave in hertz? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Frequency counts cycles per second: f = cycles/time = 15 crests / 3.0 s = 5.0 Hz. Verified the other way: 5.0 Hz multiplied by 3.0 s returns the 15 crests that were counted. The trap is dividing 3.0 s by 15 crests, giving 0.20 s per crest, which is the period and not the frequency.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish amplitude changes from frequency and speed changes
questions.stem: A radio is turned up louder without any change to the drive frequency reaching the speaker. Which statement describes the sound that results?

options.text: The amplitude rises but the frequency holds
The amplitude and the frequency both rise

options.text: The frequency rises but the amplitude holds
options.misconception: believes loudness is produced by speeding up the vibration

options.text: The wavelength shrinks as the sound grows
options.misconception: believes amplitude changes the wavelength at fixed speed

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: find wavelength from wave speed and frequency
questions.stem: A sound wave in air travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength in metres?

options.misconception: inverts the relation and divides frequency by wave speed
drops a factor of two by halving the frequency without rescaling
multiplies speed by frequency instead of dividing

questions.explanation: The fundamental relation is v = f times wavelength, so wavelength = v/f = 340 m/s divided by 170 Hz = 2.0 m. Check the second way: 170 Hz multiplied by 2.0 m equals the stated 340 m/s. The trap is inverting the ratio to f/v = 0.5 m, which has units of time and so cannot be a length.
questions.hint: Rearrange v = f times wavelength to isolate the wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: find wave speed from frequency and wavelength
questions.stem: A wave on a rope has a frequency of 25.0 Hz and a wavelength of 8.0 m. What is the speed of the wave in metres per second?

options.misconception: divides wavelength by frequency instead of multiplying
adds frequency and wavelength as if they were compatible
inverts both steps, effectively multiplying frequency by wavelength twice

questions.explanation: Speed is the product of frequency and wavelength: v = f times wavelength = 25.0 Hz times 8.0 m = 200 m/s. Verified by division in the other direction: 200 m/s divided by 8.0 m returns 25.0 Hz, matching the given frequency. The trap divides, 8.0 m / 25.0 Hz = 0.32 s, which is a period, and a period is not a speed.
questions.hint: Speed is the product, not the quotient, of frequency and wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: convert between period and frequency
questions.stem: A tone has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is the period of the oscillation in milliseconds? Report the number only.

The trap multiplies instead, 250 times 0.0040 would be nonsense, or reads the reciprocal 250 ms off the digits without dividing by 1000.

questions.learningObjective: apply inverse frequency-wavelength scaling at fixed speed
questions.stem: A string of fixed length carries waves at 300 m/s. At 100 Hz the standing wavelength is 3.0 m. The driver is raised to 200 Hz at the same tension. What is the new wavelength?

scales wavelength directly with frequency instead of inversely
halves twice, applying the inverse factor to an already halved value

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why frequency is unchanged when a wave enters a new medium
questions.stem: A tuning fork vibrating at 500 Hz is held above a water surface and then lowered into the water. As the wave passes from air into water, what happens to the frequency?

options.text: It stays at 500 Hz while the speed drops
It stays at 500 Hz while the speed rises
options.misconception: believes water is a faster medium for sound than air

options.text: It falls with the drop in wave speed
options.misconception: believes the medium redetermines the source frequency

options.text: It rises in step with the wave speed
options.misconception: believes speed and frequency always move together

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Comparing wave speeds in two media
questions.learningObjective: rank wave speeds in different media from measured wavelengths
questions.stem: One 50 Hz source drives waves in two media. Medium A shows a wavelength of 4.0 m and medium B shows 2.0 m. What is the ratio of the speed in medium A to the speed in medium B?

options.misconception: inverts the ratio when asked for A over B
reports the raw wavelength ratio without any frequency reasoning
squares the wavelength ratio by multiplying both wavelengths

questions.explanation: With one shared frequency, speed tracks wavelength: v_A = 50 Hz times 4.0 m = 200 m/s and v_B = 50 Hz times 2.0 m = 100 m/s, so v_A/v_B = 200/100 = 2.0. Second route: because f is common it cancels, leaving 4.0 m / 2.0 m = 2.0. The trap is 0.5, which reports B over A and reverses the order the question asked for.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: relate linear mass density to wave speed at fixed tension
questions.stem: Two ropes are made of the same material and held at the same tension, but one is much thicker. How does the wave speed on the thicker rope compare with the thinner one?

options.text: The thicker rope carries the wave more slowly
The thicker rope carries the wave more quickly
options.misconception: believes more material means more inertia to move forward faster

options.text: Both ropes carry the wave at the same speed
options.misconception: assumes identical material alone fixes the wave speed

options.text: The thicker rope changes the wave's frequency
options.misconception: believes the rope thickness retunes the driving frequency

The trap is the intuition that more mass helps the wave along, but the extra mass per length is inertia the wave must accelerate, so it slows down while the source frequency stays put.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: use a round-trip travel time to find a reflector distance
questions.stem: A sonar pulse in seawater travels at 1500 m/s and its echo returns 0.50 s after it is sent. How far away is the reflecting object in metres? Report the number only.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: classify interference as constructive or destructive from path difference
questions.stem: Two in-phase sources emit waves of wavelength 2.0 m. At a point where the path difference from the two sources is 3.0 m, what kind of interference occurs?

options.text: Destructive interference
Constructive interference
options.misconception: treats any overlap of two in-phase sources as reinforcing

options.text: Complete cancellation forever
options.misconception: believes out-of-phase meeting destroys both waves permanently

options.text: No interference at all
options.misconception: believes two waves only interact if they share a medium

questions.explanation: Constructive interference needs a whole-number multiple of the wavelength and destructive needs a half-integer one. Here the path difference is 3.0 m / 2.0 m = 1.5 wavelengths, that is 1.5 = 1 + 0.5 wavelengths, so a crest from one source meets a trough from the other and the displacements subtract. The trap is 2.0 m, which is a whole wavelength, but the question gives 3.0 m and 1.5 is not a whole number.
questions.hint: Express the path difference in wavelengths and check for a half-integer.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what happens to pulses after they overlap and separate
questions.stem: Two pulses travelling toward each other on the same rope overlap and interfere briefly, then move apart. What do the pulses look like after they pass through one another?

options.text: Each pulse continues with its original shape
The pulses fuse into one larger pulse
options.misconception: believes overlapping waves merge permanently into one

options.text: The pulses shrink as energy is destroyed
options.misconception: believes interference consumes the energy of both pulses

options.text: The pulses return reversed and smaller
options.misconception: believes passing through a wave flips a pulse's direction and size

questions.explanation: The superposition principle says the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements, and linearity means each wave keeps its own identity: a 3.0 cm crest passing a 2.0 cm crest momentarily gives 5.0 cm, then the 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm pulses re-emerge unchanged. The trap is the fusion answer, which mistakes a momentary sum of displacements for a permanent merger of the two waves.
questions.hint: Sum the displacements only while the pulses overlap.

questions.learningObjective: compute the beat frequency from two close frequencies
questions.stem: Two tones of 440 Hz and 466 Hz are sounded together on the same speaker. What is the beat frequency in hertz? Report the number only.

Second method: 440 Hz + 26 Hz = 466 Hz, so the beat frequency reconstructs the upper tone exactly. The trap multiplies, 440 times 466 gives a meaningless huge number, or adds to 906 Hz which is the sum tone, not the beat.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: add amplitudes for in-phase superposing waves
questions.stem: A 2.0 cm amplitude wave and a 3.0 cm amplitude wave overlap with the two crests arriving at exactly the same moment. What is the amplitude of the resultant wave at that instant?

options.text: 5.0 cm
1.0 cm
options.misconception: always subtracts amplitudes, even when crests align in phase

options.text: 6.0 cm
options.misconception: adds the amplitudes twice over for a double-counted sum

options.text: 2.5 cm
options.misconception: averages the two amplitudes instead of summing them

questions.explanation: Superposition adds the displacements, so crest on crest gives 2.0 cm + 3.0 cm = 5.0 cm, and the energy that scales with amplitude squared rises as 5.0 squared against 3.0 squared. The trap averages to 2.5 cm, which is the mean, not the resultant.
questions.hint: In phase means the displacements point the same way, so add them.

questions.learningObjective: test which measured frequency-wavelength pair matches a known speed

50 Hz and 4.0 m

options.misconception: adds frequency and wavelength values and treats the sum as the speed

options.text: 100 Hz and 2.0 m
options.misconception: assumes the highest frequency must pair with the measured speed

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: describe particle motion at a node of a standing wave
questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave pattern. At a node of that pattern, what is the particle motion like?

options.text: The displacement there is always zero
The displacement there is always maximum
options.misconception: confuses a node with an antinode of the standing wave

options.text: The particle there moves twice as fast
options.misconception: believes a node doubles the particle speed because it is a fixed point

options.text: The particle there never returns to rest
options.misconception: confuses a node of zero amplitude with permanent oscillation

The trap is the maximum answer, which describes an antinode, where the two crests add to 4.0 cm.
questions.hint: Two equal waves travelling opposite ways meet at a node. Add them.

questions.learningObjective: compute the fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends
questions.stem: A string of length 1.20 m is fixed at both ends and waves on it travel at 600 m/s. What is the fundamental frequency of the string in hertz? Report the number only.

questions.learningObjective: judge a claim that interfering waves are destroyed
questions.stem: A student claims that when two equal waves meet exactly out of phase, both waves are destroyed and never reappear further along. Evaluate that claim.

options.text: False: the waves pass on, the cancellation is local
True: the amplitudes subtract and vanish for good
options.misconception: believes destructive interference consumes both waves

options.text: True: the medium absorbs both waves entirely
options.misconception: believes the medium soaks up interfering waves as a loss

options.text: False: the waves slow down where they cancel
options.misconception: believes a zero point also slows the travelling waves

questions.explanation: Interference obeys superposition, so +2.0 cm plus -2.0 cm gives 0 cm at that point and nowhere else, and the two 2.0 cm waves keep travelling at 340 m/s with all their energy redistributed to the points where they reinforce. The trap is the true option, which treats a local zero as a global loss; the second false option is also wrong because cancellation changes displacement, never the speed.
questions.hint: Check whether anything downstream is missing, or only one point reads zero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Judging a claim about speed and pitch
questions.learningObjective: separate a speed claim from a pitch claim when judging an argument
questions.stem: A student claims that a violin string cut a little shorter sounds faster as well as higher, on the grounds that a faster wave must be a higher tone. Evaluate the claim.

options.text: Half right: pitch rises, wave speed holds
Fully right: the shorter string runs faster
options.misconception: believes cutting a string tightens it and raises its wave speed

options.text: Half right: speed rises, the pitch holds
options.misconception: believes a shorter string gives a faster wave at the same pitch

options.text: Fully wrong: neither pitch nor speed changes
options.misconception: believes a shorter string is acoustically identical to a longer one

questions.explanation: Shortening a string while holding tension and mass density fixed leaves v = sqrt(T/mu) unchanged, so the speed stays put, but the shorter length forces a shorter fundamental wavelength, 2L, and a higher f = v/(2L). With L cut from 0.32 m to 0.30 m at 300 m/s, f rises from 469 Hz to 500 Hz while the speed is 300 m/s either way, so the pitch claim is right and the speed claim is wrong.
questions.hint: Compute v from the string relation, then f from v over twice the length.
